JUST MY OPINION

The Devil’s Daughter is a pretty solid story about how Sherlock Holmes excels at everything except being a father. Although told in the tradition of Sir Arthur Conan Doyle’s novels, it’s a bit of a departure from the classic tales. The game is broken up into five investigation cases that are initially quite interesting and provocative, but sometimes end up a little borderline ludicrous. I enjoyed them, for the most part. I would argue that the ending to the second case is… bad. Nonsensical, doesn’t suit Sherlock Holmes. Etc.

I think the game’s biggest strength is its environmental design. The visual presentation, especially of interiors, is beautiful. Everything is so impressively detailed and the world feels very real and lived in.

The voice work is very good, overall.

These are all of the positive things I have to say about the game. And I am giving the game a positive review because I personally enjoyed it, but to be honest, the negatives are overwhelming.

There are some animation issues, general jankiness, horrible framerate issues, long load times, and the strange problem of an offset cursor when playing in a 21:9 aspect ratio. I hit a point in the game when I could not pass a series of QTEs and had to switch to a 16:9 aspect ratio. Took me ages to even figure out what the issue was; haven’t run into this before.

My biggest complaint is gameplay. The game suffers from lack of identity.  It couldn’t seem to decide between being a traditional slow-paced, cerebral point-and-click detective game, and being an action-packed Guy Ritchie’s ‘Sherlock’-inspired visual novel (in the style of a Telltale or David Cage game). As a result, both aspects suffer.

The game doesn’t do much to test your intelligence or give you any agency. Solving cases isn’t particularly challenging. It’s a bit rigid and hand-holdy at times. You cannot exit a location until you’ve found all clues, even if you’ve already figured everything out and have no need of any piddly inconsequential clue in the room you may have looked over. Puzzles aren’t challenging either and aren’t typically well-designed. Some are good, but for the most part it’s trial and error. 

The point & click gameplay is broken up with the inclusion of godawful minigames. I appreciate the creativity but creativity isn’t good enough. A lot of them were a bit too gimmicky (a chimney sweeping minigame inside of a stealth minigame, where you gotta climb the chimney before the orphan dies? say what?) and most of them were really not fun and some were even frustrating. Pretty much all of them are skippable (I played about half, skipped the crummier ones), which makes me wonder how confident the devs felt about them. 

Then the game tries to add action sequences anywhere it can. Too many scripted set pieces with QTEs. It honestly took me out of the game.

TL;DR terrible gameplay, good everything else. For me, this doesn’t break a game. For many it does. 

Also, there’s a sewer level with a puzzle with levers and water levels and sh*t and like WTF dude why

I just barely recommend this game. If I could go neutral, I would. The gameplay is good, enjoyable as well. However, there are several issues:

1) It's got far too many QTEs and random generic AAA game challenges in, and far less of the actual crime investigating of the previous games.
2) It ignores rule 1 of Sherlock Holmes: there is never a supernatural explaination. Without giving too much away, you have to deal with the actual occult, magical puzzles that somehow draw you into a scale model, where you can look into the past and get the answers you need to solve a case.
3) Some lines of investigations are total red herrings, and are not at all explainable outside of "trying to make someone look guilty for no reason".

I myself rather enjoyed Crimes and Punishments, since it was finding out clues, and using those clues to further your investigation rather than "work out how to get across this tile puzzle" or "avoid this big rock", which have nothing to do with the case and you don't really feel like there's any point to except to fill out time and space where the devs couldn't be arsed to actually produce content.

An honest review. (UPDATED 2)

I wanted to like this game. I wanted to, because I'm a fan of Sherlock Holmes, as imagined by Arthur Conan-Doyle. I've just recently played Crimes and Punishments for the first time and boy did I enjoy it. Obviously, I said, The Devil's Daughter will continue the same excellent formula of its predecessor. Boy, was I wrong.

So with the good first - the graphics are excellent. Everything is as good looking and better as C&P. Dynamic lights, shadows, beautiful locales, a lot of style to it all and it's a pleasure to the eye, for a while anyway. The deduction board is there, and so is Toby. 

The problem with this game is the actual gameplay. The cases are simple and poorly written, especially compared to C&P and the Testament of Sherlock Holmes. In fact, there is barely any actual "detecting" going on, as the game pretty much leads you by the nose through rushed stories, increasingly annoying QT minigames which invoke images from Indiana Jones in the most unfortunate of ways, that are clearly there as a filler for otherwise poor writing that lacks depth and development. 

Conversations are stubs, it's almost a throwback to the 90s; Holmes and Watson may as well be perfect strangers as they barely exchange words with each other. There are no interesting puzzles, most of them will make you wonder why you're playing these run-dodge-dodge-run games on bridges and forests and collapsing floors. This does not have RD Jr's charm, and after a couple of cases you start asking yourself if you even care, and you will end up skipping more "puzzles" than you solve. For a game about Sherlock Holmes, it's shockingly uninspired. 

The voice-work is barely passable, and a big step down compared to the excellent voice-work done in the previous games in the series. The dialogue is very bare-bones, and lacks depth. Lacking depth seems to be the best way to describe The Devil's Daughter. Such a shame. 

I don't know if the developers read these reviews, but if they do, I suggest they sit down and re-read Sherlock Holmes. Maybe that will put them back on track of who and what Sherlock Holmes is. This, unfortunately, isn't it. This almost feels like Frogware just said "f#$k it, they will buy anything we give them". Oh, and Holmes in this game is just a douche. Not even a charming one.

UPDATE 2: age of characters

It is true that in the source material Sherlock Holmes and Dr. Watson DO meet each other first when they are most likely in their early 30ies. But let's not be distracted by this fact - the real reason for younger characters in this game is to justify the running/jumping sequences, that for obvious reasons wouldn't be possible for older characters. Chronologically, this makes no sense either. Trying to channel Guy Ritchie's Sherlock Holmes movies is a dumb idea. If I wanted to play running and jumping in Victorian London, I would be playing Assassin's Creed Syndicate. But this is a Sherlock Holmes game. SHERLOCK HOLMES. It should be a game of wits and rich dialogue, not jumping obstacles. 

 

I DO NOT recommend this game. Buy Crimes & Punishments and Testament instead. 

Score: barely 6/10.

[u] Gameplay [/u]

Like its predecessor Sherlock Holmes: Crimes & Punishments, the majority of the game involves exploring crime scenes and examining clues. Once discovered, clues are added to a "deduction board", a gameplay mechanic which involves linking pieces of information together, leading to possibilities for different deductions. Once deductions are connected together, the player will have a full tree of deductions in the player's memory called mind palace. Depending on how players interpret the clues, they will arrive at different conclusions. Thus, the player can fail or succeed in finding the culprit.

the characters...

however, this is a forgivable crime... IF the characters were preserved, but-
- this has also got to be one of the most out of character and obnoxious adaptations of Holmes ever made, beaten only by BBC Sherlock. he's honestly unrecognizable as this character in this way- i dont begrudge him emotions, no, in fact that sort of thing is very in character, but their execution.... his behavior (both in game and implied past)... its just a complete butchering. Frogwares clearly did not want Sherlock Holmes, the detective- they wanted Sherlock Holmes, the Cool Action Hero [spoiler]Generic Single Father[/spoiler] man, and it was done so, so bad. its so bad. hes done so dirty its almost obscene
- the other characters that you are forced to interact with regularly are the most obnoxious, one-dimensional sons of bitches ever conceived, save maybe Lestrade and Wiggins (if they even count), and you will only grow to hate them, whether youre supposed to or not, and always in the wrong ways. there is no one in this game to care about, to relate to, to enjoy- theyre all terrible.

its honestly incredibly disappointing to watch Frogwares go from Crime and Punishments, which while not perfect was certainly a very fun game and a well set up detective piece, to Devil's Daughter, which is all around terrible with none of the charm of their previous work whatsoever. you can see in every aspect of it why they did what they did, at least intellectually; they wanted a more generically appealing game in an attempt to sell to a wider audience, so they tried to hit all the beats of a Generic Sells Well Game, but to do so to a Sherlock Holmes *detective* game is such a stupid move, and it was so poorly done, that i cant imagine why they ever thought it was a good idea.

I've been a fan of Sherlock Holmes since my father introduced me to the stories in my early childhood, and I immensely enjoyed the previous installments in the game series, especially the brilliant "Crimes and Punishments".

Therefore I am sad to say that this game has very little to do with the beloved character. 

I was warned before purchase that the game had taken a more "modern" approach to the gameplay, and featured some action sequences.

I went into the game expecting this. 
I wasn't even bothered by the less faithful portrayal of Sherlock Holmes as a character. What truly put me off were the puzzles, or rather, the lack of them.
 
Instead of a "few" action sequences, the game revolves almost entirely around minigames, QTEs, trial and error timed action puzzles, and illogical narrative sequences; such as the [spoiler]awful Indiana Jones style action chapter that takes place entirely in Sherlock's imagination[/spoiler].
I feel like with this game Frogwares has forgotten what makes the Sherlock Holmes series so great and unique. His use of deduction to eliminate false leads, his methodical and calculative approach to every person and situation, his ability to piece together clues from the tiniest observations, eventually leading him to the only remaining logical solution.

The game starts off on a promising note. It is beautiful for an adventure game, with several open locations to explore, full of atmosphere. Unfortunately, these locations end up being reused to the point where they lose their charm quickly, and even the first episode ends in an action sequence which reveals the villain without any real deduction from the player.

In a strange way this game almost feels like an old action adventure platformer game, the kind with simple "push the block" puzzles, and "react or die" style gameplay. Even the dialogues end up resolving themselves with very little thought required of the player. There are no real meaningful consequences to making the wrong choices.

The few logical puzzles that the game contains feel repetitive and unoriginal. Compared to the variety and ingenuity seen in "Crimes and Punishments", I quickly found myself bored with the bland assortment of puzzles this game had to offer. The few times I had to pay attention was more due to the lack of explanation in game mechanics, than due to the actual puzzle difficulty.

I'd only recommend this game to those who go into it expecting a more linear narrative experience, similar to the Telltale games. Fans of the recent Sherlock Holmes movie adaptations would likely enjoy this. If you want logical puzzles, and a true Arthur Conan Doyle style Sherlock Holmes experience, I'd avoid this and play "Crimes and Punishments" instead - assuming you haven't already done so.

All in all the game itself isn't terrible for what it is. If I could give a neutral rating, I would. I'm sure there are many people who will enjoy it for the atmosphere and storytelling. It's just not what I was expecting of a Sherlock Holmes game.

[h1]Sherlock Holmes: The Devil’s Daughter — 2 Hour Review[/h1]

[b]Playtime at review:[/b] ~2 hours  
[b]Engine:[/b] Unreal Engine 3  
[b]Verdict:[/b] Mixed / leaning negative  

I went into this knowing it’s an older game, but what surprised me most isn’t just the gameplay — it’s how clearly the [b]engine[/b] influences both performance and design.

Out of the last [b]6 games I bought, 4 use Unreal Engine[/b]. I don’t believe in conspiracies, but at some point you can’t help noticing patterns. It almost feels like Unreal became the default answer to everything, and games started inheriting the same problems along with the convenience.

This one runs on [b]Unreal Engine 3[/b], and you can absolutely feel it.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Performance & Engine Behavior (UE3)[/h2]

This game behaves very differently from modern UE4/UE5 titles:

[list]
[*]Very heavy CPU usage (often up to ~90%)
[*]Relatively low GPU usage
[*]Feels CPU-bound when new scenes or assets are rendered
[/list]

That [i]has[/i] to be a UE3 thing. Newer Unreal games usually hammer the GPU instead — sometimes to disastrous results.

The important part:  
[b]Even at high CPU load, the game stayed playable.[/b]

For comparison, I’ve had [i]Dead Island 2[/i] (UE4) drop to [b]4 FPS[/b] on my system. This game never did that. So ironically, for [b]older GPUs[/b], this might actually be the better-behaving Unreal game.

[b]My setup:[/b]
[list]
[*]GTX 1080
[*]Older CPU (clearly the bottleneck here)
[*]Linux via Proton
[/list]

No crashes, no insane stutter, no slideshow moments. Not great efficiency — but stable.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Gameplay: identity crisis[/h2]

The core Sherlock Holmes systems are still here:

[list]
[*]Crime scene investigation
[*]Clue collection
[*]Deduction board / mind palace
[/list]

And when the game focuses on those, it works.

The problem is that it [b]constantly interrupts itself[/b] with:

[list]
[*]Mini-games
[*]QTE-style sequences
[*]Timing mechanics
[*]Action and stealth sections
[/list]

Some of these are skippable — which honestly feels like the developers admitting they don’t really belong here.

This is a detective game, but it keeps trying to be:
[list]
[*]An action-adventure
[*]A stealth game
[*]A mini-game collection
[/list]

It never fully commits to being a proper detective experience.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Mini-games: not broken, just misplaced[/h2]

Not all mini-games are terrible.

I played a lawn-bowling-style mini-game:
[list]
[*]It worked
[*]It wasn’t frustrating
[*]I won 2–1
[/list]

So credit where it’s due — mechanically, some of them are fine.

But they don’t [b]belong[/b] in a Sherlock Holmes game. Less mechanics would honestly make the game feel more believable. At times it even looks like characters (or animals) interact with the world in unnatural ways, breaking immersion completely.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Writing & tone (early hours)[/h2]

After two hours, Sherlock already feels… off.

Instead of a calm, calculating observer, he often comes across as:
[list]
[*]Too reactive
[*]Too action-oriented
[*]Less methodical than expected
[/list]

This lines up with a lot of long-time fan criticism, and I understand it now.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Unreal Engine fatigue (a broader observation)[/h2]

Playing many Unreal Engine games back-to-back makes certain things impossible to ignore:

[list]
[*]Similar animation stiffness
[*]Familiar camera behavior
[*]Shared performance quirks
[*]Repeated design shortcuts
[/list]

Unreal makes it easy to ship games — maybe [i]too[/i] easy. And sometimes it feels like the engine is doing more of the design work than the developers themselves.

Again, not a conspiracy — just a pattern.

[h3]This is not a detective game. This is torture.[/h3]

I have closed one case, out of many, I assume, and I have had enough. Every detail feels wrong. Let me explain what this game did wrong in two words:

[b]ABUSIVE HANDHOLDING[/b]

You know, a true detective game, or maybe just my weird expectation of one, is a game where you actually do detective work. You investigate things, draw conclusions, and your knowledge moves the story forward. Knowledge.

Here, the game moves you forward, explains every little step you have to take, and if you want any freedom of choice, exploration, or investigation, you will find nothing.

I found a note about a missing person, and it even had an address! Of course I want to go there, it is literally on the next street. But no, there is a padlock in the way, and you cannot get to house number 5 because the street somehow ends at 9. Your clues are not yours. You have to do what the game tells you to do. Or suffer.

You know what I really have to do? Activate Sherlock's spider-sense and pixel-hunt around a location I already spent the last 20 minutes walking through without any luck. I do not remember signing up for a hidden object game.

That is why I call it abusive. The game not only forces you to follow its strict plot, it also mocks your detective skills by putting you through tedious exploration. Not careful note-reading, not actual deduction, just clicking on everything and hoping Sherlock finally says out loud what you already figured out.

The deduction system is still completely wrong. You click through a bunch of tags like a character from Idiocracy. Connecting the dots only counts when the game wants it to, not when it happens naturally because you actually followed the story and figured things out on your own. You have to build this whole rigid hierarchy as if only two things can be related at a time, otherwise the full picture cannot be restored.

You know what game does [b]DEDUCTION[/b] correctly? [b]DUCK DETECTIVE![/b]
That game was funny, clumsy, and childish, but you still had to reach conclusions based on your [b]own[/b] analysis. Here, you just turn off your brain and play mini-games.

OH YES, MINI-GAMES!

I hate them with a pure passion. This is exactly how not to do mini-games in a detective game. They are either annoying or just stupid and boring. Looking through 5+ keyholes, clicking on garbage, and listening to Sherlock say "just garbage" five times in a row. What a meta-commentary. I had the exact same thought while playing this game.

Then the game suddenly tries to become some kind of GTA-style chase sequence, or The Witcher 3 with magical detective vision guiding you through swamps. And the most absurd thing of all is [b]PLAYING AS A DOG[/b]. Hilarious. Sherlock stays behind, but I have one question: how does the dog manage to open doors?! It has paws! It cannot open doors like that!

I do not understand the tone at all. Sometimes the game tries to be overly realistic. Fine, children, let us take a blood sample and mix it with three different liquids. For each liquid, you have to click three times. Rinse and repeat. And then suddenly the DOG MAGICALLY OPENS DOORS.

[i]"Detective" as a genre was butchered.
"Adventure" will make you die of boredom.
"Mystery" will not be yours to solve.
"Puzzle" means hunting for pixels.
"Story Rich" is nowhere near enough to justify everything else.[/i]

This was achieved doing different things across the game, from placing and object in a certain place, to smelling  a tobacco pouch to identify its brand, to throwing an harpoon on a pig (long story) to know more about a killer. All this was just the starting point, then you had your detective sense, which enabled you to find hidden prints of missing objects, and then you had your clues screen in which you associated different facts, like it was part of your brain,  and ideas about the case flowed along until you reach one of many deductions to find the resolution.

Worlds apart from the rest of this franchise, which began as a point-and-click adventure/puzzle game. I don't mean that in a good way. Logic has been replaced by trite puzzles, mystery has been replaced by detective novel cliches, and the rest of the game is comprised of irritating action sequences. "Crimes and Punishments" was beginning to diverge from the series' formula, but it managed to entertain and not annoy too much. Not this installment. I don't buy Sherlock Holmes games to play through (unskippable, may I add) faux-"Uncharted" action sequences. Why can I skip the puzzles but not those? The best part is the deduction mechanic of working through collected information and linking it, then forming assumptions, and the moral choice system (as in "Crimes and Punishments"). However these systems are sorely underused, they should be the main focus of the game, not diverted from by those (yes I really, really hate them) action sequences. Storyline-wise, it falls into the modern fashion of making Holmes a rugged brawler *before* a gentleman investigator, opting for the Cool Holmes over the traditional character (as previous games used). His daughter is back again, a plot I always thought was the weakest and most "fan fiction"-like in the series. Watson has been relegated to mostly a prop. It's not a very elaborate or unique Holmes plot, which makes playing through the tedious bits even more of a chore since there is no narrative pay-off. [h1]In-Depth Review[/h1]

[h3]Visuals[/h3]
Characters might look a bit weird due to their blurry texture whenever you see them up close, but they still look decent otherwise. The backgrounds look realistic with the varied interior and city landscapes, although I admit that the map can be too vast for its own good. I tend to get lost whenever I step outside the building and never dared to step outside anymore unless necessary because of it.

[h3]Story[/h3]
The story seems to be a continuation of another [b]Sherlock Holmes[/b] game made by [url=https://store.steampowered.com/developer/Frogwares][i]Frogwares[/i][/url]. I never played any of their [b]Sherlock Holmes[/b] games before, and since the story proceeds after an event in the previous game, I didn't understand what happened whenever it mentioned those events. Luckily, the game never focused more on this except on the beginning and the end of the story, which also helps to clear the context somewhere in between due to the revelations.

The case itself is alright. I did manage to deduce most of the perpetrators correctly, although I found it hard to figure out how one of the perps manage to do their crimes. It seems that the game wants to make it look as if you are always "correct" in solving the case because they never provide a summary of how the perp killed the victim. You also have options to either jail or let them go, which leads to different cutscenes.

[h3]The Game[/h3]
[b]Gameplay[/b]
The game is played like point-and-click games, except that you are moving your character with the keyboard. You'll be able to interact with any objects to gather clues and use an ability that allows you to see other things that can be missed with the naked eye. It's not a hint system though. You'll need to use this to collect different clues, so expect to explore the whole area at least twice to get all clues that you can get. However, there isn't a hint system in case you are stuck. Most of my playtime was spent roaming around the area several times just to figure out which clues that I missed since the game apparently won't let me proceed with the story if I missed any.

Puzzles, minigames, and QTEs are abundant in the game, allowing you to play different things to proceed with the story. They are usually unique and easy to finish, although I found that the ones in the second case to be difficult to solve. Moreover, the lockpicking minigame can also give some trouble due to its controls. I still didn't get used to its controls even after I finished the game.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2609814791 

You need to make hypotheses based on the available facts, where you often have to choose between two choices to deduce the perp. Most of these decisions are usually quite vague since you need to pick up subtle hints given by the game. Understanding the suspects' personalities, motives, and backgrounds is needed for this, and solving the case will be more or less of a guessing game if you don't get them right.

[b]Length and Difficulty[/b]
I finished the game with all achievements in 11.5h. I found that finishing the puzzles to be hard compared to solving the case, but you can always skip them if you want. However, doing so might ruin your gameplay experience due to them being abundant in your playthrough. Sometimes, I even thought that there are just too many "actions" and moving around in the game compared to the solving case, and the loading screen is way too slow if you like to run back and forth between places.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2609815535 

[b]Problems[/b]
The game stutters a bit when I played it. It doesn't happen that often though. The character's movements are also stiff since they might stop walking or correct their positions.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
The game might be of high quality, but I found it to be lacking a hint option to make them more enjoyable. A lot of puzzles can be difficult to solve, and there is no hint or whatsoever that can help you to solve them. There's only a skip button, which is not fun to use all the time. That being aside, some puzzles are easy and fun to solve.

Despite it being a continuation of another game, you still can enjoy it without playing the first one if you don't mind brushing off some facts. Some events might be too vague to you although they will be revealed in time.

To be honest, I didn't enjoy the game at first, especially because of the second chapter that has nothing but frustration in almost everything that it had, but I ended up enjoying the game because of the following chapters. I still had difficulties in collecting all clues, but it becomes more tolerable after I knew some subtle hints that were given from the game. I won't recommend buying this at full price, but make sure to wait for a big sale before picking it up - the base price is way too expensive.

Short version:
Pros:
+ Very charming protagonist
+ Interesting cases with substantially diverse gameplay, “mini-games” and puzzles
+ Mostly decent voice acting
+ Solid presentation
 
Cons:
- Lackluster finale with a poorly developed antagonist
- Some voice acting is spotty
- A bit janky (gameplay and animations)
 
“Long” version:
[u]Sherlock Holmes: The Devil’s Daughter[/u] is a story-driven puzzle and mystery-solving game where you play as the titular Mr. Holmes. You must comb through several crime scenes, uncover clues, do some research and interview suspects in order to solve cases.
 
The story is alright. While all five cases are somewhat “connected” by loose ends from previous ones, the self-contained stories of each investigation are more interesting. The only exception to this is that the final investigation is based on a poorly developed side plot that feels forced and features the worst characters of the game, ending the adventure on a whimper. Then again, I am not an avid Sherlock Holmes connoisseur, therefore some easter eggs and references might have gone over my head.
 
The characters are not particularly well-developed but some of them are likeable.
Holmes is the clear standout - as he should be. He is charismatic and has a subtle air of cockiness about him. Watson and a few side characters have a friendly and helpful demeanor but nothing more.
Unfortunately, all other characters have some vague personality traits and not much else – the eccentric millionaire who acts suspicious and will clearly backstab you, the mysterious neighbor who plays the victim and will obviously double-cross you… The list goes on.
Watson gets benched on several occasions and most interactable NPCs are information dumpers with little to no characterization.
 
My main gripe about the story, again, is the disappointing finale, which focuses on the two worst characters of the entire game. Both walk the line between annoying and completely obnoxious and I found my emotional investment to be nonexistent during the final act. It does not help that both these characters’ voice acting is subpar (more on that later).
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2868557187
Gameplay-wise, [u]Sherlock Holmes: The Devil’s Daughter[/u] offers a lot of variety.
While combing for clues in a crime scene is your usual “click here to interact” with very light puzzle-solving, a lot of the side activities are diverse. You might need to open a door with a lockpick, which will start a shape-based puzzle, but interacting with another object will give you an entirely different action to perform. There are also mini-games that must be completed to move the story forward. These are never great, as the gameplay is quite archaic and easy, but they are usually over very quickly and are seldomly repeated. I found them to be a nice change of pace.
Interviews are also a big part of the game, but choice does not really play a part in them. You can explore all dialogue options without repercussion.
 
While some of the gameplay I mentioned has extra features, like mashing a button or picking between two deductions when checking for clues, these are all very minor, inconsequential and can be overlooked in this review.
 
You also get to control a few characters other than Sherlock for very short sequences and puzzles but, gameplay-wise, it is all the same.
 
After gathering enough clues and interviewing everyone, you will be able to open a deduction tab and combine several known facts and try to conclude who the killer is. Sometimes, said deductions and combinations do not make a ton of sense or are basically a guessing game, but they are rather obvious for the most part. This feature was really interesting, as different choices might grant you distinct outcomes. You might not even find out who the killer is!
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2850889671
When it comes to the graphics, I feel like [u]Sherlock Holmes: The Devil’s Daughter[/u] is very solid.
The visuals are clearly not the sharpest, as you can definitely see that it does not have the budget of a triple-A game; however, the art direction and world-building are strong.
The world feels lived-in and cohesive and there are many NPCs populating the streets and the places you visit.
The character models are serviceable for NPCs, but the main characters are a bit more detailed.
Some of the animations are on the lackluster side; the camera often turns away from character actions to avoid having to show certain animations, like characters changing outfits, for instance. On the other hand, when you fast travel, the game really goes for atmosphere and you get treated to some quaint “loading screens” where you are in a carriage on your way to your destination and you can take out your notebook and check current objectives, clues, etc. Really awesome attention to detail and it also keeps you distracted.
 
Sound is up next.
I have no strong opinions about the soundtrack, mostly because of how unremarkable and generic it is. It does its job, I guess.
 
On the other hand, sound effects are consistent and plentiful. The ambient sounds are really good and help you feel immersed, whereas louder, more aggressive sounds pack a punch.
 
Voice acting is a mixed bag. While I certainly adored Holmes and Watson’s voice acting – even when some of the writing was questionable – you also get your fair share of campy delivery.
Unfortunately, two other main characters are played by actors that are either miscast or not really into selling the performance. They sounded like AI trying to sound human and it just deterred from the overall enjoyment of any scene they were a part of. I am being vague because I would most likely spoil a few plot points by discussing their identity.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2868557538
All-in-all I found [u]Sherlock Holmes: The Devil’s Daughter[/u] to be a very enjoyable but flawed experience. I liked the overall story, despite a few loathsome characters; the gameplay was fine, as I found myself doing new things for a large portion of the puzzles – were these sections super fleshed out? Did they feature precise controls? Not particularly, but there was so much gameplay diversity that it never grew stale. I completed one case a day (total of five cases) and it took me around 14 hours to beat the entire campaign.
I do not consider it to be very replayable, as moral choices are inconsequential and only change the final few lines of dialogue for each case.
 
Thus [u]Sherlock Holmes: The Devil’s Daughter[/u] is definitely worth trying if you enjoy solving mysteries and murders. An easy recommendation on a sale.
 
Final score: 7.5 out of 10.

I have so much to say about this game, and I'm not sure how to begin. No spoilers in this review.

I enjoyed piecing together larger events and crime scenes. For each case, they update your footwork just enough to keep it fresh. Some of the action sequences are entertaining and very Holmesian. 

That being said, The Devil's Daughter really misses the mark in several areas.

The gameplay tried to be a little too fresh. They couldn't seem to decide whether they were making a Sherlock Holmes game or an Assassin's Creed game. Taking cover around corners, climbing over rooftops, tailing people so they don't see you, elaborate spacial puzzles in tombs and sewers, and even using eagle vision--it felt like a ripoff, and in more ways than one. Firstly, they couldn't think of gameplay more stimulating than outright copying Assassin's Creed; second, of all things to copy into a Sherlock Holmes game, that's a weird one; third, the Assassin's Creed-like gameplay is thick enough that it makes it abundantly clear that it exists to distract you from the fact that the writers did a poor job on all of the mysteries.

And oh boy, did they do a poor job of the mysteries. Not a single case had a difficult deduction. Not one! I didn't struggle over the conclusion whatsoever. It required no serious thought or time to discover the culprit. Instead, the game focuses on your MORAL decision surrounding the culprit, such as whether to imprison them or absolve them, and emphasizes (weakly) the moral consequences surrounding your detective work.

I'd just like to emphasize that again: they made a Sherlock Holmes game where the mysteries are child's play, and instead focused on making you feel bad for arresting or not arresting someone.

When I signed up for a Sherlock Holmes game, I signed up for a mystery. An actual deductive mystery, as promised. Not "Assassin's Creed with a vision board."

AGAIN: NO CONCLUSIONS ARE DIFFICULT IN THE SLIGHTEST SENSE. IN A SHERLOCK HOLMES GAME.

To make it all even worse, just to end on a nice sour note, the climax at the end of the game simply ends. There is no let down, no epilogue. Just lengthy climax, a solution is presented, then the end. Not only can they not write a mystery, apparently they can't even follow the basics of story writing.

If you are bad at deduction and mysteries and you like to play endless dungeon puzzles and hide-and-seek with patrolling guards, this is the game for you.

For those looking for a good adventure and detective game, I would have to say that you will enjoy this game, it has a more refined story comparative to the earlier games in the series. The makers went for more drama and action, and tried to keep the game flowing yet include puzzles that would work on the gamer's mind. I found some of the puzzles to to a bit to fictional in terms of would someone actually design a place this way, but most of the puzzles had logic to them. I was able to finish the game without having to look up hints, and even if you do get stuck the game lets you "skip" the puzzle in order to continue, but you should never really need to other then maybe the last puzzle. The story is great, in follows the aftermath of the books and ties in "Family" really well. They went for mystic and supernatural near the end of the game which was welcome. I did find that the later cases felt rushed and short compared to the first half of the game, which let me down, as it didn't explore what could have been great cases. Graphics are good, as good as your gonna find in this type of game, sound and music were also ok, nothing great but enough detail that it didn't feel cheap.

Should you buy this game, I would say yes, it plays like a book and fans of the books or those wanting to use your mind will find something here, I enjoyed my playthrough of the game, and say it was worth my time.

Why, Frogwares ? I thought we were friends.

Some people may remember playing Super Mario Bros 2, a hundred years ago. Some may even have noticed, even as a kid back then, that "2" was a weird game compared to every other in the series. And then years later we all found out that the reason SMB2 felt odd and out of place was that it was a reskin of a completely different game, where they'd only replaced the main characters' sprites and [spoiler]tacked a Mario-is-dreaming (SPOILER ALERT!) scene at the end[/spoiler].

This is a bit what Devil's Daughter is like, except they didn't even use the right sprites.

Were the game titled "Fetlock Burns & The Devil's Daughter", telling the deeds of young american action hero Fetlock Burns, for some reason on holiday in England and staying at Sherlock Holmes' old address, it would be fairer to the player.
Because in no way, and from no angle, is the guy you move around Sherlock Holmes.
It would be bad enough if the difference (with popular culture) was limited to the looks (and the voice, and for God's sake the accent), but also gone are the wits, demeanour, dryness of analysis and lovable brand of light autism we all have admired and enjoyed for decades in Sir Conan Doyle's works.
Fetlock is just "some dude", and talks and acts like he's in a family sitcom on cable in 2010.
There is enough to say about Watson alone to fill a page, but I will let that one slide in view of all the rest.

In the game you lead him (Fetlock) in a series of events that are more tailored to Lara Croft or Batman than to a victorian gentleman (which is ok, since Fetlock is an american acrobat adventurer), while the screen is cluttered with the instructions for the current minigame - and it is a flurry, as these minigames just keep on coming, one after another.
Occasionally the flow of poorly jointed minigames will be interrupted by a brief session of guessing, where you will connect at times contrived observations and clues, through no particular logic, to form "Conclusions" which are too often open to interpretation. At any rate, you do more running than reasoning.

The puzzles themselves, that is the few that are not based on jumping around and avoiding traps, are too often absolutely arbitrary, and to "solve" them you have to guess by trial and error what the designer meant the solution to be. While this is an issue that plagues all puzzle games on occasion, in DD it compounds with all the other shortcomings to deliver a deeply unsatisfactory solving experience. Other times they are not puzzling at all, unless you can consider pressing clearly marked buttons in sequence from 1 to 10 "a puzzle".
The other kind of "puzzle", of which there is way too much for a SH game, is often padded and repetitive but never entertaining.


But enough of singing praise.

The game is short, less than 10 hours, and divided into 4 separate cases (the first of which you should guess the gist of within about 20 seconds), with some background noise-like "main plot".
The ending of each case comes up abruptly once you have collected all clues, and you have to pick a culprit among your suspects based on loose logic that you had no real part in devising or applying.

Loading times are pretty long, and you sometimes are made to go back and forth between locations with no real necessity. And frankly, Fetlock's book is (not that much) funny the first time you see it, but after 500 cab trips you have to wonder if he's learning to read from scratch from it, or if each time it has a different comic book hidden inside.

The writing is poor. I kept on playing hoping for the game to fall back by mistake on the right track, only to see Fetlock act out another uncharacteristic, american everydude dialogue. I won't even touch the plot, that is subjective and some may even like it. Stranger things have happened, like the mayor of Burgundy's self combustion in 1453.

In the end, if you make a real effort to ignore every time someone says "Holmes", and stick to thinking you're Fetlock with all your mental might, it is merely a poorly executed mixture of Tomb Raider and the CSI games, rather than a blotch in a series we have come to love and anticipate in spite of its slip-ups.

Couple of additional minor details that grate hugely :
- at some point you may find a map leading to money. On the map, there is a currency symbol. It is all but "£".
- Fetlock dresses like a hobo. A victorian gentleman would not dream of being seen in the street so attired.

What the game ultimately does is raise the question of why Frogwares would take such a dump onto an intellectual property that they seemed to hold dear all these years, with all its ups and downs.
Various reasons, that come arbitrarily to mind if I turn on my detective mode, may or may not include:
- a major wave of ministrokes
- the replacement of all writing staff at FW with people who have never read a book (never mind a SH book)
- the new publisher buying all FW's bank debt and forcing them to make this drivel against their will
- FW having it up to here with SH games and wanting to end the series in a way that would slight SH fans the most.

Graphics are good !

Worth acquiring ?
IF you are NOT looking for a SH game, maybe, and possibly if you are 13.
A profound unfamiliarity with the subject matter may help its enjoyment.

If you look to play SH games, play Crimes and Punishments instead. If you already finished C&P and want to pick this up then heed my warning:

- The cases are worse. Much worse. There is only one case which is short and on point and which I enjoyed immensely while the other 3 are either too railroaded or downright improbable. The second case is egregious and laughable in the worst way as the final conclusion simply doesn't make sense. The final "case" is a short resolution to the overarching plot which is featured much more prominently in this game than in C&P and it suuuucks. 
- Minigames are much more prominent and it feels like the devs decided to make you do more immediate puzzle-solving instead of writing complicated cases requiring a bit more brainwork. The puzzles are easy but way overused and the sequences are just too long dragging on forever before returning to the routine.
- Some minigames are literally trial and error this time around, especially scripted action sequences and choose the right dialog. The save system requires you to restart the whole thing if you don't choose the right option (without any clue) which is terrible design. The ending sequence is just daft in that sense.

This is a weird regression for SH games. Instead of making a game about SH cases and doubling down on what's good in them: gathering clues, interrogating suspects, making conclusions and actually "think", the devs decided to dumb the whole thing down with minigames and instead of believable cases it's all about shock value. Exorcism, trailing criminals, sneaking past guards, talking with the dead, exploring Mayan pyramid (for way too much time). 

This is not what SH is about and is not a strength of this game. If before mini-games were only a supplement to casework, this feels like a collection of minigames with veneer of cases to make you choose lockpicks for nth time. Simplicity is underrated, all we need is a 3-pipe problem. Get this on deep discount if you really want liked C&P and the minigame parts of it.

[u]TL:DR - If you liked 2014's Crimes and Punishment, you should buy this as it has the same very enjoyable gameplay formula. That said, it lacks polish: storylines and dialogue feel more rushed, and minigames are frustratingly clunky.[/u]

[h1]The Good[/h1]
[list]
[*]The winning formula of 2014's C&P - i.e. episodic format, deductions interface and slow-motion observations that really makes you feel like a detective - is back, and works really well,
[*]Also back is your Telltale-style ability to decide the guilty party in each case, as well as their fate, and compare your decisions with others. IMO this is what elevates it above a normal adventure game. 
[*]Graphics are great - some are complaining about loading times but they're no longer than C&P were, and at least you're in the cab and can look at your evidence/deductions while it loads.
[*]The storylines are varied and interesting with a lot of promise - they're just rushed (see below).
[/list]

[h1]The Not So Good[/h1]
[list]
[*]You get thrown into some truly horrible minigames with clunky controls and virtually no explanation as to what to do - plus, in some cases these aren't skippable. It feels like a misguided attempt to liven up the gameplay, but there's no need, as the deductions/clue hunting and dialogue options are much more entertaining.
[*]The storylines feel rushed: there's too little scene-setting, exposition, dialogue, and explanation of characters' motives. I still have absolutely no idea what the motivation of the first case's guilty party was. It feels like the developers spent more time on the above-mentioned minigames than the story aspect, which should be at the heart of this game.
[*]Saves are through checkpoint, which wouldn't be so bad if the unskippable mingames weren't horrendously clunky.
[/list]

Crimes and Punishments is great. With it Frogwares have created not just the best game they ever made, not just the best Sherlock Holmes game, but one of the best examples of adventure games in recent history, if not of all time. For some reason, 2 years later they followed up with The Devil's Daughter, which isn't the worst game in their Sherlock Holmes series, but is very close to being one.

Using the same overall structure ideas and a lot of mechanics, Sherlock Holmes: The Devil's Daughter could be an improvement, an evolution, or a really interesting experiment of change. The team clearly aimed at the latter, but failed spectacularly. They changed the looks and personalities of Holmes and Watson, this time basing them on the Guy Ritchie movies - Watson looks almost exactly like Jude Law, while Holmes doesn't resemble Robert Downey Jr. visually as much, but is animated to look like he's being played by the named actor. The story attempts to be more "personal" and continues from the horribly stupid plot point of the ending of The Testament of Sherlock Holmes, which I was hoping, would be forgotten, but no - Holmes has a daughter now (who's actually Moriarty's daughter), and is emotionally highly unstable when it comes to the topic. And the overall tone and speed of cases is meant to be much more action heavy. And none of that works. Well, okay, 1 thing works - Watson feels less stupid than he sometimes appears to be in books and previous games, but even there - you don't really spend a lot of time with him in this game.
  
In fact, it's hard to say with whom and with what you spend most of the time. Very first case, for example, spends couple dozen minutes on a stealth section as Wiggins (one of the homeless helpers for Holmes). Then case ends on an escape scene which more or less resolves itself, without you doing much deducting. Next case opens with an extremely boring sports minigame and then spends half an hour in an imaginary Mayan temple, bad puzzles and Indiana Jones references. And those goddamn minigames... Even though I got a bit bored of lock-picking in Crimes and Punishments by the end, it never felt like it was pushing it, never felt like it was out of place. On the contrary, most of the content of The Devil's Daughter is based around these mostly pointless mostly skippable minigames and QTE-like sequences that just do not work. There's a sequence that tries to use the Holmes' intelligence in a fight scene, again emulating Ritchie's movies, but it's all bad guesswork and poorly conveyed controls that work at random in the very same scene. And don't even get me started on the "push the heavy object" puzzles, where even if you figured out what to do, you still have to wait through the agonizing minutes of pushing stuff.
  
There are attempts of expanding and improving on Crimes and Punishments, but those do not work either. You have more choice in analyzing people, but it's either an obvious choice, or a pure guess on player's part, which improves nothing. Visuals have been refined, but actually make some of the same locations between both games look less memorable and more blurry. Moral choices, which didn't really play a big story part in the previous game and were there to fit Holmes' character and give players more agency, are tied to the ending somewhat. But given that this whole thing is based around the horribly written and executed "Holmes has a daughter he cares about a lot for some reason", it's a moot addition. There are a few good puzzles that expand on the ideas of the previous games, but they are so few and sometimes poorly implemented as well, that it doesn't save the game.

I fully support the idea of experimenting with Sherlock Holmes, especially after reaching such a high point as Crimes and Punishments was. In fact, as I've said many years ago, I'd love to see a modern take on Sherlock from Frogwares (Though the example I used last time, BBC's Sherlock, has since went to crap). But Sherlock Holmes: The Devil's Daughter is a poor execution of a bad idea and a failed experiment. It lost almost everything that made the series Sherlock Holmes and is extremely not fun to play. Whenever the studio returns to the character, I hope they do something else with it.

Another great Sherlock Holmes game.  I'm not sure why these get mixed reviews from critics.  They are some of my favorite games.  This one has the best graphics yet.  Amazing attention to detail.  You really feel like you're there.  The voice acting is not as good as Crimes and Punishments, though.  I can't think why they changed the voice actors for Holmes and Watson.  The new Holmes is fine (although I have a fondness for the orginal) but I can't stand the new Watson.  And the voice actress for Kate is gratingly bad.  I also don't care for decreasing the ages of Holmes and Watson since clearly this game comes after the previous installments.  The storyline functions very much as a capstone for the detective as he deals with problems he created as a young man.  So why is he illustrated as a young man?

The stories are good.  I particularly like how the individual cases are related thematically to the main case.  It fills out that case more, which is necessary because it is bizarrely the briefest of the stories.  And yet you're always thinking about it.  The smaller cases are all very good, except for a Study in Green, which I give a mixed review to.  It had a lot of fun things to do as far as minigames and such, but I found the resolution to be bizarre and unlikely.

Speaking of the minigames they are great.  A lot of ingenuity there and much better than previous games in the series.  I would like it if the detective portion of the game were harder.  Even if it were impossibly hard.  The basic idea of this and the last one is that you can possibly finger the wrong suspect, but since you always find all of the clues, you are nearly guaranteed to come up with the correct option.  It would be nice if it were possible to over look something.  Perhaps if you leave an area without finding everything, things will change by the time you go back or maybe following up one lead might keep you from following up on another.  Things to explore in future installments.

I still love the moral decisions they are the best part.  In the case with the accident it was very difficult for me.  A lot of people had died because of the man's actions, and by putting you in the middle of the carnage the game really manipulated your feelings.  I won't talk about why I am conflicted about the resolution for fear of giving away spoilers but I would enjoy talking to someone else who has played the game.

First and foremost, it's important to note that, while skipping mini-games or OTEs is available in this game, doing so will result in missing their associated achievements. 

So, if you're aiming for 100% completion, don’t skip them and remember that those tasks need to be completed manually; otherwise, you’ll end up wasting a massive amount of time replaying them later on (trust me, I learned this the hard way T^T).

This is one of the easiest games in the Sherlock Holmes series. It's great for beginners or anyone not used to this type of game, since it offers a lot of help, such as skip options, very obvious object highlighting, and clear instructions on what to do and how to progress (or even hold your hand and walk with you). 

Also, unlike the others in the same series, the puzzles here don’t test your skills or brainpower at all. You just need to collect all the clues and use a bit of logic to put everything together at the end. If you’ve played older Sherlock Holmes games or even 'Chapter One', you’ll find this one much more beginner-friendly and guided.

 I packed up the foundry in the second game where the steps are incredibly complicated and it finishes with a running sequence where you have to balance using the mouse in one hand and the keyboard in another which I find quite impossible. I played "Sherlock Holmes: The Devil's Daughter" after "The Testament of Sherlock Holmes" and after "Crimes and Punishments". I haven't played any other Sherlock Holmes game yet. While all three are pretty good and a experience i don't want to miss, i would say "The Devil's Daughter" is somewhere between the two others. More in the direction of "The Testament of Sherlock Holmes", than the exeptional "Crimes and Punishment". Actually it feels more like a Telltale Game. Heavy story-based, deductions and puzzle elements and a lot of action and QTEs. 

1. Sound and voice acting is good, for some exceptions
2. The darkest theme i encountered in the series so far. 
3. Great setting in old London.
4. While it is the newest installment (2016), the graphics dosen't add up to it unfortunately.
5. A lot of action and QTEs involed, which is the biggest flaw the game have. QTEs should not be in any game and because it is a consol port the action isn't really for PC controls. It's still ok, but it could be a lot better. 
6. Some mini-games are fun, while others are just annoying.
7. Puzzles are a lot easier than previous titles and so are the deductions. It is a lot easier to get to the right conclusion, than "Crimes and Punishment" for instance.
8. Story is great and the cases are a little bit more connected to each other. Or at least parts of them. 4 out of the 5 cases are pretty great.

You can play previous installments of the game, if you want to find some connections to past cases.

I’d happily give this game a [b]balanced 5/10[/b], but I rated it “[b]No[/b],” so I’m not going to totally recommend it—[b]especially not at full price[/b]. Read why.
[hr][/hr][h2][b]Gameplay & Difficulty[/b][/h2]
This game took a [b]major downgrade[/b] from [i]Crimes and Punishments[/i] in terms of gameplay. There’s not much detective stuff going on, and most of the time you’re just left clueless about what to do next.

Yes, they added a [b]Master Sleuth[/b] difficulty—but what’s the point, really? If you're spoon-fed with vague details and solving nonsensical minigames, then it doesn’t matter how hard it is.

[h3]Stealth Segments[/h3]
The stealth mini-games? They’re simple, stretched out, and completely unnecessary. It feels like they just added this section to make your playthrough longer. Only one stealth section had any real investigative action—and that’s sad. If I wanted full stealth, I’d go play [i]Dishonored[/i].

[h3]Quick-Time Events[/h3]
To be fair, I enjoyed most of the QTEs—but they had [b]zero detective value[/b]. They’re more about reflexes than reasoning. Imagine how cool it could’ve been if they followed the [b]RDJ Sherlock[/b] route—where you construct the future possible outcomes based on your own deductions against your opponent's actions all within a constructed time-frame. But no, they went with button mashing instead.

[h2][b]Minigames Breakdown[/b][/h2]
There is [b]way too much trial and error[/b] in the minigames. It’s frustrating and honestly outrageous. This is [b]Sherlock Holmes[/b], not some random guy throwing darts blindfolded. You're supposed to feel [i]clever[/i], not [i]lucky[/i].

[h3][b]Character Portraits[/b][/h3]
This part was actually a great improvement. Not all deductions are handed to you—you need to piece together context and evidence manually. My only gripe? You can see the first letter and length of blurred answers, which basically gives it away. Either blur it better, or remove it altogether.

[h3][b]Toby Sniffing[/b][/h3]
Okay, I can’t hate on being a dog. But honestly, I’m glad they did less of this (sorry Toby!). It’s straightforward: follow the scent, boom, done. They could’ve made it more interesting by adding [b]intersecting scent trails[/b] and giving Toby a chance to do his own deductions. Y’know—show us why he’s [i]the best nose in the British Empire[/i].

[h2][b]Characters[/b][/h2]
Why do [b]Sherlock and Watson[/b] look younger here than they did in [i]Crimes and Punishments[/i]? Aren’t they supposed to be in their mid-40s or 50s by now?

The voice actors are also different—maybe a budget issue? I don’t hate the new ones; they did a decent job. But the [b]Sherlock[/b] in [i]Crimes and Punishment[/i] just had that cynical, humorous tone I really miss.

[b]Watson[/b] is practically absent. Same with [b]Lestrade[/b]. What’s the point of a [i]Sherlock Holmes[/i] game if the key supporting characters don’t do anything? In [i]Crimes and Punishments[/i], [b]Watson[/b] had proper screentime, showing both his medical and military side. Here? He’s just… a doctor. [b]Lestrade[/b], for some reason, acts super suspicious. I honestly thought that was part of the plot, but it’s not.

[h2][b]Cases & Storyline[/b][/h2]
There are six cases total, and most of them are just unclear. The cases don’t feel like standalone mysteries anymore—they’re overshadowed by a forced main plot. One moment you’re solving a crime. The next, you’re thrown into another storyline. It’s jarring.

The cases are often confusing, short, and vague. You’re left [i]guessing[/i] because the game doesn’t give you solid clues. It’s more like [i]“Sherlock Holmes: Gut Feeling Edition”[/i] than any actual deduction.

There were moments where I was just like, [i]“That’s it?”[/i] Literally. I could summarize whole cases with that line.

[h2][b]Visuals & Performance[/b][/h2]
Here’s where the game actually shines a little.

The visuals are better than [i]Crimes and Punishments[/i], with more detail and better lighting. But it loses that mystique atmosphere the previous game nailed so well. The ambience just isn’t the same.

Performance-wise, [b]no crashes[/b] for me. Played on high settings—but there were [b]occasional FPS drops[/b] in specific scenes. And no, it’s not just me—other players reported this too.

The [b]controls are clunky[/b], especially when interacting with objects. Sometimes Sherlock just jolts onto a table or gets stuck in weird corners. Very immersion-breaking.

[h2][b]Music & Sounds[/b][/h2]
This part is honestly excellent. The sound design is enhanced from [i]Crimes and Punishment[/i]—which is impressive, considering the previous game already nailed it. You’ll hear creaks, street noise, vendors, kids, bugs, and all that ambient city stuff.

The music is very fitting for each case. It brings that enigmatic energy the game promises—at least in this department, they delivered.

Frogwares has made many Sherlock Holmes games, but this is the first one by them that I've tried and I enjoyed it. The game consists of 5 main cases for us to solve, following one after another. The 5 cases aren't related to one another, but there are personal problems in Sherlock's life that keep coming up while we're solving them, which eventually culminate as the 5th case that we undertake.

There are different things that we do whilst solving the cases. There are dialogues with characters, where we need to listen to them and at times point out if something they say contradicts found evidence. There is exploration of course, a major aspect of the gameplay. When exploring, the plot takes us to different locations, both indoors and outdoors, where we need to interact with key pieces of the environment and gather clues.

On many occasions we need to solve puzzles and engage in mini-games (such as lockpicking). The game gives us a choice to skip the puzzles if we wish, though they're all worth giving a go and majority aren't frustrating. During action sequences, there are QTEs. I am not normally a fan of these, though most of them in this game aren't too hard, and if we fail one, it just takes us to the start of the scene, so we don't really lose any major progress. There is also one stealth section in the game too, which too can be skipped if necessary. However, I found it to be quite fun and atmospheric, and it doesn't overstay its welcome.

One of the most important aspects of gameplay is gathering clues, putting them together, and finally making logical deductions. When making deductions, some of them can be mutually exclusive, so we can fiddle with different "what if" possibilities to see what new deductions can be made. Eventually these lead us to who is guilty. However, beware, because the game allows incorrect deductions to lead us to incorrect conclusions and actually end up accusing an innocent character. Pretty much each case has one guilty party and at least 2-3 innocent ones that can be accused. Once we have decided on who to convict, we can either choose a harsh punishment and send them to jail or absolve them by just getting them psychiatric help or something similar. The game allows us to continue onto the next case even if we convicted an innocent person. Cruel but realistic. That's what choice and consequence should be about. Although would've been nice to have more repercussions for these choices in future cases.

The game is pretty linear, and although some outdoor locations are a bit sizeable, there isn't much to do in them, so there's no reason to explore any areas unless the case requires us to do it. And I personally prefer that, because vast open worlds slow down the pacing and take our attention away from the story. The visuals are pretty decent for a game that came out in 2016. All characters and scenes are fully voice-acted and the voice acting is really good in my opinion.

Generally I really enjoyed the game and solving the cases. Particularly the second case (A study in green) was my favourite of the lot as the plot in it hooked me. Although I personally think the game should've done away with a few sections, such as the imagined Mayan temple full of deadly puzzles which really did not need to be that long and tedious, or the section where we need to explore the sewers and fiddle about with water levels in it to get further. 

Other than a few tedious parts, I had fun and was hooked on the story. Going to check out another Sherlock Holmes game by these developers.

[h1] PROS: [/h1]
[list]
    [*] 5 interesting cases, each with its own unique story and mystery.
    [*] Decent graphics that still hold up reasonably well.
    [*] Good voice acting that helps bring the characters to life.
    [*] You can customize and disguise Sherlock, which adds a bit of fun and variety.
    [*] Moral choices at the end of each case.
    [*] Some genuinely clever puzzles and deductions that make you feel like a detective.
    [*] The investigation mechanics become more enjoyable once you understand how the game works.
[/list]

[h1] CONS: [/h1]
[list]
    [*] Whoever designed the first case deserves to be forced to play it for 100000 years! The forest chase sequence combined with the awful controls is incredibly frustrating and nearly made me quit the game.
    [*] Terrible camera handling and controls. It takes a long time to get used to them, and they never feel truly comfortable.
    [*] The game often hides progression behind tiny, easy-to-miss details. For example, you may find a postcard containing all the information you need, but the game refuses to progress until you inspect the back and make a specific deduction.
    [*] The highlighting feature is not very helpful, as many important objects are still difficult to spot.
    [*] Sherlock is surprisingly unlikeable at times and often comes across as a complete jerk.
    [*] A ridiculous amount of QTE events.
    [*] Lots of loading screens when fast traveling.
    [*] Some puzzles are poorly designed and simply not fun. Pushing boxes around at a snail's pace or following barely visible scent trails while playing as a dog quickly becomes tedious.
    [*] The autosave system can be frustrating and often saves at the worst possible moments.
    [*] Certain obstacle room puzzles rely more on trial and error than actual problem solving.
    [*] The game occasionally mistakes pixel hunting for detective work.
[/list]

[h1] OVERALL: [/h1]
This game has a lot of flaws, and honestly the first case almost made me quit more times than I can count. Between the clunky controls, frustrating chase sequences, and obscure objectives, the opening hours are easily the worst part of the experience.

However, once you get past that rough start, the game becomes surprisingly enjoyable. The cases become more interesting, the mysteries are engaging, and the deduction system starts to shine. While the gameplay is often held back by questionable design decisions, there is still a solid detective adventure hidden underneath all the frustration.

I bought the game for around 5€ during a sale, and that's exactly how I would recommend getting it. At a heavily discounted price, it's worth experiencing for the stories and investigations alone. I've played every Sherlock game by Frogwares and was unfortunately disappointed by this one. Not that it was a bad game, but more that it could have been the best that they've made so far. Crimes and Punishments/Testament are up there as the two best games in my opinion.

This game feels like it's having an identity crisis. It's torn between the riveting deduction/puzzle element shown in Crimes and Punishments, and expanding its gameplay mechanics to attract a larger customer base. In my opinion, this game does not do this right at all. At one point I felt like I was playing Crash Bandicoot in the temple, the following scene it was Deus Ex in the graveyard, and then it was like Amnesia in the sewers, trying to control the water flow to get by. If I wanted a platformer/stealth/action game, there are many to compete with on the market, and Frogwares can't compete with all three genres. 

Personally, I feel future titles should stick to the tenets of Crimes and Punishments but expand on them. Keep it to puzzles and deductions please! Bring back the morality system and actually give it a use! I really liked how in this game the finale touches on whether you killed or absolved the first case perpetrator or rightfully arrested other cases' perpetrators; perhaps let your morality or honour dictate how future characters see you and talk to you in future games!

The character designs are gorgeous and the voice acting far superior to past games. Sherlock now seems like the cool guy you wouldn't mind having a drink with in the pub as he tells you stories, and the action scenes with him are very cool. However, he is meant to be a "high-functioning sociopath" and is traditionally portrayed as an awkward character with little empathy for others. This is only a minor niggle for me. 

The atmosphere is brilliant. I love piecing together the clues while eerie music is playing in the deduction scene, or looking through suspects' belongings as the mysterious music chimes. I'm not too fond of the mini games however. They teach ypu to box, and you have no boxing scenes in the game. You play lawn bowls, but you don't play this minigame again. It just feels like a bunch of flash miniclip games thrown at you; you're learning skills and never get the chance to use them again. 

Altogether, I'd recommend the game but only on a good sale. It's roughly 10 hours' long, the game does tell great stories and the atmosphere built is brilliant. You can skip some of the annoying segments of the game but I personally grinded them out and used a walkthrough so I wouldn't have to be stuck for long, which is a massive shame. My friend loves Sherlock Holmes and quit this game altogether by Case 3. 

Rant over, here's my verdict:

Pros: atmosphere, story, retained the excellent deduction system, nice overarching storyline threaded across all five cases with their own stories to solve, sherlock and watson are cool stuff

Cons: Identity crisis (trying to appeal to a larger customer base with minigames that just frustrate the current fanbase who are here for the puzzle/riddle elements), one case makes no sense (to solve a case, you "enter" a temple and witness what happens inside, but how can you accuse someone as a result because it was all in your head, sherlock.), sherlock seems too caring for others (his daughter, fair enough as she is a loved one of his, but he also seems genuinely caring for the kid in the first case; he's an awkward sociopath who should care more about the thrilling case).

Buy it on a sale. A good sale, ideally. I did enjoy most of this game to be fair but Frogwares need to sort out how they go from here before they sleepwalk into mediocrity.

Devil's Daughter is another worthy addition to the Sherlock Holmes series. It consists of 5 major cases, plus the unfolding of the story of Kate's daughter (who was introduced in Testament). It uses the newer 'mind palace' interface and the graphics and audio are on par with the later titles.  For those who have played other Sherlock Holmes games, It is an enjoyable interlude in a familiar place. The apartment at 221 Baker and Scotland Yard remain unchanged and, of course, Toby (the dog) is always present.

There are some very complex puzzles in diverse environments that I found challenging and fun. Lots of evidence to uncover and multiple suspects in each case. Achievement hunters should be able to get 100% if nothing is skipped and you are able to win a lawn bowling tournament (which was simpler than I expected).  Unlike some of the other games, there is no achievement for identifying the 'correct' suspect or making specific moral choices. This gives the player more freedom in linking evidence and coming to their own conclusions. I played the game on the easier level, as I was looking for relaxation rather than stress. Even on easy, you can still die but the penalty is marginal (restart at the same place).

There were a couple of balancing ('walk-the-plank') and eavesdropping exercises that I could not do with my keyboard and mouse. A controller was more intuitive for me to manage two-handed coordination. 

The game auto-saves at regular intervals during each case. Thus, if you want to return to a prior checkpoint in the current case, you can do so. Once a case is completed, you are warned that moving ahead will delete all saves and begin again with the new case. Until this point, you can circle back and revise your conclusion and choices without penalty.

A warning... if the Holmes story grabs you, it is possible to binge for weeks by playing one game after another.  I am not sure why it took me so long to jump into this world but it has been fun and I still have more titles to play. I highly recommend this to those who enjoy a good story and love solving mysteries.

Unfortunately, there are a lot of problems. Apparently, the dev's main attempt at game improvement since C&P revolves around one concept: MORE! More minigames, more action sequences, more QTEs, much longer puzzles. As a result, many of the minigames and action sequences are long and tedious. The minigames can at least be skipped, but the action scenes cannot. Unfortunately, these don't rely on logic. They rely on repeated trial and error, and then memorising the right sequence of things to do. It's a memory game, not a logical one, and I hate it. Even the minigames that are fun at first long overstay their welcome.

In addition, the things that should have been improved were not: the faces are still wooden and lacking in animation; the voice acting is significantly worse than C&P (and it wasn't particularly good in the first place); and the deduction interface is still clunky.

The highest difficulty is not well-thought out. Adding a timer to everything or shortening the window to do a QTE is a lazy way to make things harder. For example, you can miss QTE prompts to challenge a suspect's statement since the QTE ends WHILE the suspect is still speaking. How are you supposed to know to challenge a lie if they don't even get to finish it??

Finally, for the love of god, a notice all devs: PLEASE let us disable vibration on controller. Many of us hate playing with it on, and it is obnoxious to force us to use it because you can't be arsed to include this in the settings.

Overall, I recommend against this game.

Some rough edges notwithstanding, I confess that I quite liked [i]Sherlock Holmes: The Devil's Daughter[/i]; building on the strengths of [i]Crime and Punishments[/i], it felt like a more fully realized game in many ways.

Times are busy for the detectives of 221B Baker's Street. Taking place after the short story, "The Final Problem," Holmes's days of criminal investigations are made more complicated by the presence of his adoptive daughter, Katie Holmes, and a new neighboring tenant who knows that Kate is actually Professor Moriarty's daughter. Though the bulk of the game concerns five separate investigations that are otherwise unlinked, the tenuous relationship between Holmes and Kate does a lot to create a more holistic experience, adding a thematic backbone to the otherwise procedural affairs. Admittedly, this does cause the game to fall firmly in that oh-so-maligned school of games derided for their "dad-ification" of the medium, but it also works here to both make Holmes feel more human [i]and[/i] to escalate the stakes of the overall narrative.

Mechanically, things are familiar for fans of previous Frogwares games. Playing primarily like a point-and-click adventure, players collect evidence in the environment by logically deducing how clues fit together and through a variety of sundry minigames. These minigames are... harder to ignore this time around, though, and I suspect that's why many players have a more strongly negative reaction to this game than the previous title. You can smell money being spent on the cinematic presentation here, and there's no sequence that the developers don't attempt to spruce up with a minigame or lovingly animated cutscenes throughout. That said, they suit the more bombastic tone of the game; [i]The Devil's Daughter[/i] feels much more like a penny dreadful than the previous Holmes title, which erred closer to the original Sir Arthur Conan Doyle short stories and novellas.

And there, perhaps, is the rub. This Sherlock Holmes game is much louder and more energetic than its predecessor, and with that come the narrative complications that upset matters. While everything feels more broadly escalated, the pacing is also more abrupt and everything is presented with a more explosive quality. These faults and deviations in presentation do a lot to grab the player's attention, but I personally found them to ultimately be in service to the much more tightly scripted writing. If the previous title struggled to justify the name [i]Crime and Punishments[/i], this sequel earns its title through and through.

Honestly, I think I may go against the grain here in saying that this title is slightly better than [i]Crimes and Punishments[/i], even if I do say that recognizing my own personal bias towards more melodramatic plots. Though it makes a lot of very deliberate tonal choices and concessions to a more casual audience of mystery games, I think it ultimately sticks the landing. If you've enjoyed other Frogware Sherlock Holmes games or are just looking for a compelling detective game, my recommendation to try [i]The Devil's Daughter[/i] isn't just obvious - it's elementary.

The Devil's Daughter is a detour from the traditional point-and-click style of former Sherlock Holmes games from Frogwares. This may cloud my judgement as I am used to the style of the former Sherlock games, but it is clear that they have tried to mainstream the game series to get more action-oriented gamers onboard. This may have worked, but in the process they made the puzzles less interesting and the plotline obvious. The "twist" in The Devil's Daughter is very obvious and the daughter is a very unsympathetic character, making the main story fall a little flat for me.

I enjoyed the earlier parts of the game more than the latter parts. Some of the new mechanics are interesting (like a minigame where you have to stalk someone or another where you have to run away while simultaneously making decisions on your path based on Sherlock's information), but later in the game, a lot of the puzzles become long and tedious even after the point where you have figured out how to solve them. It actually feels like some of them have been made extra long in order to stall time to make the playtime longer.

Buy this game if it is on sale, you have played all other good point-and-click/adventure games and are looking for an okay puzzle game with some quick time events (or if you are new to puzzle/adventure gaming and looking to ease into the genre as this has some action elements), but I would not buy this at full price.
